newsitem.title: USA: Oil exec sees lessons for refiners in rail mergers.
newsitem.headline: Oil exec sees lessons for refiners in rail mergers.

text.p: U.S. oil refiners, faced with poor profits and a wave of mergers, would do well to study the merger pattern of the railroads in U.S. history, an oil executive told colleagues at a refining conference here Monday.

Drawing a parallel between the two industries, he said the rail industry entered into a prolonged consolidation period after its 1880-1930 golden era ended, with the maturity of what he called the automobile era pegged at around 1980.
"The consolidation time can last for decades and will likely come in waves," said Calvin Cobb, managing director of consultancy Ernst Young/Wright Killen.

"Refining has been in consolidation for a little over 15 years and the activity has been concentrated in the early 1980s and ten years later in the early 1990s," Cobb told executives at the National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA) annual meeting.
"Currently consolidation interest is at a high level with some transactions being consummated, some pending and many others being explored," Cobb said.

Industry sources have said the number of U.S. refineries is down to about 185 from 300 in the early 1980s. The U.S. rail industry is meanwhile down to around 500 companies today from about 6,000 in the 19th century, Cobb said.

Cobb also said that over 90 percent of railroad capacity has concentrated in just 13 companies, and noted that some of those refining companies that have chosen to join the merger mania as buyers have been rewarded for their aggressiveness.
"These high performers have decided that even in a mature industry they have and will continue to find a niche or other well-defined strategic position that will create shareholder value," Cobb said.
Cobb noted those high-performing companies include Tosco Corp, Ultramar and Diamond Shamrock, which merged last year into Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Inc.
Stock analysts often point to Connecticut-based refiner Tosco as a company whose acquistions and aggressive trading have reinvented oil refining in the 1990s.
The company's stock has about quadrupled in the 1990's, during which time it has gone from being a backwater refiner to the largest U.S. independent refininer and marketer.

Part of that acquistion binge has been in marketing assets like its Circle K gasoline and convenience store chain, which parallels Cobb's observation that rail companies have expanded into other business as rail mergers have run their course.

"New directions being pursued by some (refining) companies include a shift to more intensive retail marketing, further expansion into refinery-based petrochemicals and other supply chain arrangements," Cobb said.

Cobb noted his comparative analysis of the rail and refining industries was based on research into the work of the late Russian economist Nikolai Kondratieff, who described so-called 'long wave' economic cycles of around 50 years.

"Refiners have experienced performance similar to that described by Kondratieff as the the demand for petroleum products reached maturity and the industry entered into the rationalization period," Cobb said.
-- Oliver Ludwig New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
